issues.legal_issue: An appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal may review the evidence fully and reverse the acquittal when the evidence supports guilt and the trial court’s approach was unreasonable, while giving proper consideration to the trial judge’s credibility findings, the presumption of innocence, reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s opportunity to see the witnesses.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after rejecting prosecution witnesses and the deceased’s statements on grounds the Supreme Court found erroneous.
The High Court independently assessed the evidence, accepted the prosecution witnesses and the deceased’s statements, and reversed the acquittal of the accused.
The evidence included eyewitness accounts, repeated identifications of the accused by the deceased, and medical evidence that the deceased died from acid burns.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in setting aside the acquittal because the trial court’s approach was clearly unreasonable and the evidence supported the conviction.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an appellate court has full power to review the evidence underlying an acquittal and may conclude that it should be reversed. In exercising that power, it must give proper weight to the trial judge’s views on credibility, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of any real and reasonable doubt, and the caution due when disturbing factual findings made by a judge who saw the witnesses. No earlier cases are cited in the supplied judgment.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_supports_guilt: The prosecution evidence, assessed as a whole, supports the accused’s guilt.
predicates.trial_court_rejection_was_unreasonable: The trial court rejected material prosecution evidence for reasons that were unreasonable.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the evidence supports guilt, and the trial court unreasonably rejected material evidence, the acquittal may be reversed after full review.

issues.legal_issue: The fact that prosecution witnesses are close relatives of the deceased does not, by itself, justify rejecting their testimony.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the testimony of witnesses who were related to the deceased because of that relationship.
The witnesses described the events at the scene and the deceased’s immediate identification of the person who poured acid on him.
The Supreme Court found no cogent reason to disbelieve the witnesses’ accounts.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was wrong to reject the witnesses’ evidence merely because they were related to the deceased.
issues.legal_principle: Close relatives of a deceased person would normally be reluctant to spare the real assailant and falsely identify another person; relationship alone is therefore not a sufficient reason to disbelieve their testimony. The judgment does not rely on a cited statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which witness testimony is relied on to establish responsibility for an offence.
predicates.close_relative_witnesses: One or more witnesses whose testimony is relied on are close relatives of the deceased person.
predicates.no_cogent_reason_to_disbelieve: The evidence discloses no cogent reason, apart from the witnesses’ relationship, to disbelieve their testimony.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, testimony from close relatives is not rejected solely because of their relationship when no cogent reason to disbelieve them is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A deceased person’s statements identifying the assailant may be accepted as reliable despite a claim of unconsciousness or differences in language when the evidence supports the person’s ability to make the statements and the differences are not inherently abnormal.
material_facts: After the assault, the deceased told people at the scene that the accused had poured acid on him.
The deceased later made a report and a further statement to a police officer identifying the same person.
At a dispensary, a doctor recorded another statement identifying that person and testified that the deceased was in possession of his senses.

The trial court inferred that the deceased had become unconscious and could not have made the earlier statements, but the doctor’s statement did not show that unconsciousness lasted long enough to prevent them.

The statement recorded by the doctor used more refined language than the earlier statements, but the Court found it was not unusual for the same person to use different language with different listeners.

The doctor sent the recorded statement to the magistrate on the third day, explaining that the delay resulted from workload; the statement bore the deceased’s thumb impression and the deceased was transferred soon after it was recorded.
issues.conclusion: The deceased’s statements were properly accepted; the unsupported inference of prolonged unconsciousness, the difference in language, and the explained delay in forwarding the doctor’s statement did not provide grounds to reject them.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the statements in light of the evidence about the deceased’s condition and the circumstances in which they were made. An inference that a person was unable to make an earlier statement is not justified merely by a reference to unconsciousness where the evidence does not indicate prolonged unconsciousness. Different use of colloquial and refined language by the same person is not inherently abnormal, and an explained delay in forwarding a statement does not, on its own, require an adverse inference where the surrounding circumstances support its authenticity. The judgment does not cite a statutory provision or earlier case for these assessments.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_deceased_statem: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution relies on statements made by a deceased person.
predicates.deceased_identified_assailant_consistent: The deceased identified the same person as the assailant in statements made on separate occasions.
predicates.evidence_supports_capacity_to_speak: Evidence about the deceased’s condition supports the ability to make the statements and does not establish prolonged unconsciousness preventing them.
predicates.language_difference_is_explainable: Differences in the deceased’s language across statements are consistent with ordinary variation in speech to different listeners.

issues.definition: When a criminal case relies on a deceased person’s consistent identification, the evidence supports the person’s ability to speak, and differences in language are explainable, the statements may be accepted as reliable.
